The Antica Via del Cifalco fascinates first and foremost precisely because of the mystery surrounding its very existence. How is it possible that, for a path known for hundreds of years, it has been so difficult to find written and oral sources recounting with certainty and consistency its history, its social and cultural importance, and its natural and scenic beauty?

Of the little that has been handed down to us, even less has taken root in general culture, starting with what is currently available online. Once on the spot, it was not easy to find residents who had ever heard of it or who knew anything more than that it was an old medieval mule track that went from Ponte Organasco and Barbagelata “and then down to the sea”.

So do not be surprised if, along your journey, you come across inhabitants who know nothing about it; nor if, in the works of even authoritative people who have devoted years of research to the culture and history of the Apennines between the Taro and the Scrivia, there is no reference whatsoever to the Via, beyond a few fleeting mentions of the scarce and generic information available to the general public.

The rediscovery of this route was therefore also an opportunity to carry out historical, naturalistic and cultural-anthropological research on this path and on the adjacent territories. In its small way, it sets out to enhance and bring to life an immense heritage of Apennine culture, all too often mistreated and forgotten.

In a sense, there is no history of the Antica Via del Cifalco, understood as a unified and coherent account of the path as such, that has been handed down over time. It is not known, for example, exactly when the path was created, nor when people began to call it by this name. It is, however, mentioned in an exchange of lands between the Malaspina and the de Meleto in 1251, to date the oldest historical document attesting to its existence. An old document on the boundaries of the parish of Casanova di Rovegno, held at the Episcopal Archive of Tortona, shows that in the 16th century it was still widely travelled by caravans, mules, bandits and whatnot.

The name “Cifalco” almost certainly comes from M. Gifarco, the most representative mountain of the entire route. Where this latter place name comes from is a much more open question. It would seem to derive from “Girfalco” or “Girifalco”, plural “Chifalco”, from the Old Norse “Geirfalke”, that is “gyrfalcon”; which happens to be the largest of the falcons, coming from the Arctic regions and their inaccessible cliffs, and still today the falconers’ favourite. This would support the theory that claims the presence, at some unspecified time in the past, of northern peoples who migrated from Germany and/or Scandinavia, and who are said to have bred and imported it for its aggressiveness and its exceptional hunting skills. According to legend, these peoples settled in particular at Barbagelata, which is said to owe its name precisely to the appearance of those who settled there. Rumour still has it today that the inhabitants of Barbagelata – by now rather few – have a build and stature very different from those of the people of the neighbouring villages. And so, following this trail and its suggestions, the name of the road might derive from the frequent circling of these birds of prey all along the Trebbia-Aveto ridge. In reality, the origin of the name may more simply be found in the ironic nickname with which the muleteers, in league with the local inhabitants, referred to the customs officers posted on lookout by the Malaspina lords on the summit of M. Gifarco, who watched over them like “vulture falcons”.

There are, however, other theories. In the time of the late Roman Empire, there were public officials responsible for measuring and dividing up land, who were called “gromatici”. In defining limits and boundaries they carved signs, most often in the shape of birds or other animals. Following this other trail, the name Cifalco would come from the Latin epigraphic inscription “cis falcum” (on this side of the falcon), a sign that marked the summit of a mountain. We shall stop here, but there are also other fascinating reconstructions that would, however, require more careful verification.

While it is difficult to speak of a history of the Via del Cifalco in a unified sense, there are nonetheless at least two episodes of enormous importance that have the Via as a whole as their stage (see more extensively in the section b. Historical notes on the territory). The first – as reported by the Bollettino Storico Piacentino of 1954 – concerns the fascinating and daring crossing of the Via del Cifalco by the Emperor Frederick I Barbarossa in 1167, escorted by Obizzo Malaspina and his men, reaching as far as Ponte Organasco and then continuing towards Tortona. The second has to do with the famous “Fieschi conspiracy” of 1547, in its final part, when the Fieschi family and its entourage, in the grip of despair, fled from Genoa to the Castle of Cariseto, in all likelihood along the Via del Cifalco, before moving on to Montoggio.

In this section of further reading we shall set out the essentials of what we wished, and were able, to rescue from Oblivion, referring you to the bibliography section of this site for further reading.
